v: Right now, beneath Calgary's streets, nearly thirty-three thousand of the pipes that carry sewage away from homes and buildings have passed the life that pipes like them are expected to last.
And if none were replaced, that number would more than double by twenty seventy-one. So, how old are the pipes under your feet?

The City's open data doesn't include its sewer mains, so this study looks at the connections. The City publishes the public section of each home's connection, from the main to the property line. Nearly three hundred sixty-eight thousand of them, about two thousand eight hundred kilometres of pipe.
Each record has the year the pipe went in, and what it's made of. We set each pipe's age against published service lives for its material: a short, a typical, and a long benchmark.
The typical connection went in in nineteen ninety-five, so it's thirty-one years old. But one in four is more than fifty.

Two in three are plastic, expected to last about a century. One in five is clay tile, mostly from the sixties and seventies. Cast iron, expected to last about sixty years, is three percent. And half of it is already past that.
Against the typical life for each material, about nine percent of connections are past it. Judged by the short end of the range, it's one in four. By the long end, about two percent.

One honest caveat. Four in five of the pipes past their typical life have no specific material on record, so the study gives them a cautious forty-five years. Age is a warning sign, not proof that a pipe has failed.

The oldest networks are in Calgary's established communities. Among those with at least a thousand connections, Inglewood, Renfrew and Banff Trail are oldest, with the typical pipe from the mid nineteen-fifties. In Wildwood, three in four connections are past their typical life.
In the newest communities, like Alpine Park and Glacier Ridge, the typical pipe is just two or three years old.

The bigger story is the wave behind them. The boom years of the seventies laid more connections than any decade before. As those pipes age, the count past typical life climbs. About forty-three thousand by twenty forty-six, and seventy-eight thousand by twenty seventy-one.

The City is already fixing pipes from the inside, sliding a new liner through the old one, with little or no digging. Its records list about four thousand relined connections. Seven hundred ninety-one are dated twenty twenty-five, more than three times as many as in twenty seventeen.
And residents report sewer problems. In twenty twenty-five, Calgarians made about fourteen thousand three-one-one requests about sewer back-ups, sewer maintenance and catch basins.

Calgary isn't alone. Across Canada in twenty twenty, nearly fourteen percent of smaller sewer pipes were rated poor or very poor. And a City report lists nine large wastewater river crossings, of unknown condition, among the assets whose failure would have severe consequences.

What the open data can't show is the condition of each pipe. The City reports condition only as totals, in its asset management plan, not pipe by pipe. With pipe-by-pipe inspections, age could become a true picture of risk.
